title: Iacocca Takes a One-Dollar Salary
text:
In 1978 Henry Ford II fired Lee Iacocca as president of Ford. Within months Iacocca was running Chrysler, then the third-largest American carmaker, and he soon discovered it was close to bankruptcy. It was losing hundreds of millions of dollars, its cars were selling poorly, and its management was in disarray.

In 1979 Iacocca asked the federal government for loan guarantees, a highly controversial request. He also needed to ask suppliers, banks, the United Auto Workers union and Chrysler's own managers to accept painful cuts.

To make that request credible, he cut his own salary to one dollar a year. He wrote in his autobiography that he called it "equality of sacrifice": he could not ask others to give up money unless he went first. Senior executives took pay cuts, and the union accepted concessions in wages and benefits.

Congress passed the Chrysler loan guarantee act at the end of 1979, backing 1.5 billion dollars in loans. Chrysler launched new compact cars, returned to profit, and in 1983 repaid the guaranteed loans years ahead of schedule. Iacocca became one of the most famous businessmen in America.
lesson: If you need others to sacrifice, go first and make it visible. Shared hardship is accepted; imposed hardship is resented.
source: Lee Iacocca, Iacocca: An Autobiography (1984); contemporary press reports
caveat: Iacocca also received large stock options, which later made him very rich, so his sacrifice was less total than the one-dollar figure suggests.
